studies.title: The Effects of an Oral Taurine Dose and Supplementation Period on Endurance Exercise Performance in Humans: A Meta-Analysis.
studies.abstract: Taurine is central to many physiological processes, some of which are augmented by exogenous supply and have the potential to facilitate endurance performance; however, its independent effects on performance have not been systematically analysed. To evaluate the effects of isolated oral taurine ingestion on endurance performance and to assess the contribution of (1) the dose and (2) the supplementation period to the ergogenic effect. A search was performed using various databases in September 2017. The studies were screened using search criteria for eligibility. Ten peer-reviewed articles were identified for inclusion. A sub-analysis of time-to-exhaustion (TTE) trials (n = 7) was also performed. The effects of (1) dose and (2) the acute (single dose) or chronic (> 1 day) supplementation periods were assessed using meta-regression. The doses of taurine ranged from 1 to 6 g/day and were provided in single doses and for up to 2 weeks among a range of subjects. Taurine ingestion improved overall endurance performance (Hedges' g = 0.40, 95% CI 0.12-0.67, P = 0.004), which was similar in TTE trials (Hedges' g = 0.43, 95% CI 0.12-0.75, P = 0.007). There were no differences between acute or chronic supplementation for the full sample (P = 0.897) or the TTE group (P = 0.896). The dose of taurine did not moderate its effect on endurance performance (P > 0.05). Human endurance performance can be improved by orally ingesting a single dose of taurine in varying amounts (1-6 g).

studies.title: Combined Aerobic-Resistance Training and Taurine Supplementation Reduce Asprosin and Elevate Spexin in Men with Obesity: A 12-Week Supplement-Blinded, Randomize
studies.abstract:
Aim

Asprosin, a white adipose tissue-derived glucogenic adipokine, and spexin, a satiety-promoting neuropeptide, are dysregulated in obesity, yet their collective modulation by structured exercise and nutritional supplementation remains poorly characterized. This trial investigated the effects of 12 weeks of combined aerobic-resistance training, with and without taurine supplementation, on plasma asprosin, spexin, and body composition in obese men.

Methods

Forty-four obese men (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2) were allocated in a randomized, placebo-controlled, supplement-blinded design to control plus placebo (CON), taurine supplementation alone (SUP; 3 g/day), exercise plus placebo (EX), or exercise plus taurine (EX + SUP; n = 11 per group). The 12-week protocol combined aerobic training at 60% heart rate reserve (Karvonen formula) with progressive resistance training at 60% of one-repetition maximum, with load re-estimated every four weeks. Plasma asprosin and spexin were quantified by ELISA; body fat percentage (BFP) was assessed by bioelectrical impedance analysis. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc correction and Cohen's d effect size estimation were applied throughout.

Results

Significant Group × Time interactions were detected for all five outcomes (all p < 0.05). EX + SUP generated the greatest reductions in plasma asprosin (Δ = -11.20 ng/mL, p < 0.001), body mass (Δ = -5.50 kg, p = 0.003), BMI (Δ = -1.80 kg/m2, p = 0.002), and BFP (Δ = -4.90%, p < 0.001), together with the greatest elevation in plasma spexin (Δ = +0.29 ng/mL, p < 0.001); effect sizes were large across all EX + SUP outcomes (Cohen's d = 1.17 to ≥1.87). CON showed no significant change in any variable (all p > 0.05).

Conclusions

Combined aerobic-resistance training with taurine supplementation produced statistically superior, large-magnitude improvements in adipokine regulation and body composition relative to either modality in isolation, demonstrating greater improvements in the combined intervention group compared with either modality applied independently. Given the per-group sample of n = 11, these findings should be considered preliminary and exploratory; independent replication in larger, adequately powered trials is required before any clinical translation can be considered.

studies.title: Acute Effects of Taurine Supplementation on Maximal Fat Oxidation and FATmax in Recreational Endurance Runners: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Crossover, and
studies.abstract: Taurine (TAU) has been shown to improve time to exhaustion (TTE) and fat oxidation during exercise; however, no studies have examined the effect of acute TAU supplementation on maximal fat oxidation (MFO) and related intensity to MFO (FATmax). Our study aimed to investigate the effect of acute TAU supplementation on MFO, FATmax, VO2peak, and TTE. Eleven recreationally trained male endurance runners performed three incremental running tests. The first visit included a familiarization to the test, followed by two subsequent visits in which exercise was performed 90 min after ingestion of either 6-g TAU or placebo (PLA) using a triple-blind randomized crossover design. There was no effect of TAU on MFO (p = .89, d = -0.07, TAU: 0.48 ± 0.22 g/min; PLA: 0.49 ± 0.15 g/min or FATmax (p = .26, d = -0.66; TAU: 49.17 ± 15.86 %V˙O2peak; PLA: 56.00 ± 13.27 %V˙O2peak). TTE was not significantly altered (TAU: 1,444.8 ± 88.6 s; PLA: 1,447.6 ± 87.34 s; p = .65, d = -0.04). TAU did not show any effect on V˙O2peak in comparison with PLA (TAU: 58.9 ± 8.4 ml·kg-1·min-1; PLA: 56.5 ± 5.7 ml·kg-1·min-1, p = .47, d = 0.48). However, V˙O2 was increased with TAU at most stages of exercise with large effect sizes. The acute ingestion of 6 g of TAU before exercise did not enhance MFO, FATmax, or TTE. However, it did increase the oxygen cost of running fixed intensities in recreationally trained endurance runners.

studies.title: The effects of taurine on repeat sprint cycling after low or high cadence exhaustive exercise in females.
studies.abstract: This study investigated the effects of taurine on repeated sprint exercise, performed after fixed incremental ramp exercise to exhaustion at isokinetic high (90 r/min) or low (50 r/min) cadences. In a double-blind, repeated measures design, nine females completed an incremental ramp test to volitional exhaustion, followed by 2 min active recovery and 6 × 10 s sprints on a cycle ergometer, in one of four conditions: high cadence (90 r/min) + taurine (50 mg/kg body mass); high cadence + placebo (3 mg/kg body mass maltodextrin); low cadence (50 r/min) + taurine; low cadence + placebo. Heart rate (HR) and blood lactate concentration B[La] were measured before and after the ramp test and after the sprints. Taurine lowered HR vs. placebo prior to the ramp test (P = 0.004; d = 2.1). There was an effect of condition on ramp performance (P < 0.001), with higher end-test power (d = 3.7) in taurine conditions. During repeated sprints, there was a condition × time interaction (P = 0.002), with higher peak sprint power in the placebo conditions compared to taurine (sprint 2-6; P < 0.05). B[La] was higher in taurine compared to placebo post-ramp (P = 0.004; d = 4.7). Taurine-lowered pre-exercise HR and improved incremental end-test power output, with subsequent detrimental effects on sprint performance, independent of cadence. Short endurance performance can be acutely enhanced after taurine ingestion but this effect might not be maintained across longer periods of exercise or induce the need for longer recovery periods.

studies.title: Effects of different doses of taurine supplementation on repeated-sprint performance after exhaustive exercise in a high temperature and humidity environment.
studies.abstract:
Objective

This study investigated the effects of acute pre-exercise taurine supplementation at different doses on exercise performance during exhaustive exercise and subsequent repeated sprint (RS; 6 sprints) activity in a high temperature and high humidity (HTHM) environment.

Methods

Sixteen college students (8 males and 8 females) participated in a single-blind, randomized, crossover-controlled trial. Participants completed four experimental conditions: high-dose taurine (HDG, 6g), medium-dose taurine (MDG, 4g), low-dose taurine (LDG, 1g), and placebo (PG). Sports performance, physiological responses, and subjective perceptions were assessed, including peak power (PP), mean power (MP), fatigue index (FI), reverse vertical jump (RVJ) height, time to exhaustion (ET), heart rate (HR), blood lactate (BLA), and rating of perceived exertion (RPE).

Results

During RS, PP and MP declined progressively across sprints (P < 0.05). Taurine supplementation attenuated the decline in power output compared with PG. In males, the HDG showed greater preservation of PP and MP, whereas in females, the LDG was more effective in maintaining MP, and the PG exhibited the greatest reduction in power output. Taurine supplementation increased exercise tolerance in a dose- and sex-dependent manner. ET was significantly longer in the HDG than in the PG in males, whereas in females, ET was significantly higher in the MDG compared with the PG (P < 0.05). RVJ performance decreased following exhaustive exercise in females (P < 0.05). Although no significant differences were observed in HR, BLA, or RPE among conditions, typical post-exercise response patterns were evident.

Conclusion

Acute taurine supplementation prolongs time to exhaustion and enhances repeated sprint performance in HTHM environment, with dose- and sex-specific effects.

Clinical trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06824571, January 22, 2025. Retrospectively registered.

studies.title: Effects of taurine on skeletal muscle in senescence-accelerated mice and C2C12 myoblasts and myotubes.
studies.abstract: Taurine is a semi-essential amino acid with diverse cytoprotective effects and is associated with anti-aging. This study explores the role and molecular mechanism of taurine in muscle aging. Senescence-accelerated mouse prone 8 (SAMP8) and its resistant (senescence-accelerated mouse resistant 1, SAMR1) mice were given 1% taurine water from 5 to 10 months of age, while control mice were given distilled water (DW). At 10 months of age, a rotarod test was performed to assess muscle endurance. SAMP8 mice had a shorter running time on the rotarod test than SAMR1 mice. Taurine significantly extended running time compared with that of DW-drinking group in SAMP8 mice, a similar trend was observed in SAMR1 mice. The gastrocnemius muscle was used for the RNA-sequencing analysis. Among differentially expressed genes between taurine and DW, Tbx5 and Alb showed some significant differences between the treatment by RT-qPCR. Myoblast C2C12 cells underwent cellular senescence induction with D-galactose (D-gal), which was detected by SA-β-gal staining. Taurine reduced SA-β-gal-positive area induced by D-gal, suggesting its protective effect against cellular senescence. Myotube induction was inhibited by D-gal treatment and restored by taurine, as detected by immunocytochemistry of myosin heavy chain (MHC) and Western blot of myogenin. D-gal-induced decrease trend in protein level of TBX5 was significantly increased in C2C12 myotubes treated with taurine. Taurine may have a protective effect on muscle senescence and myotube regeneration.

studies.title: Taurine deficiency as a driver of aging.
studies.abstract: Aging is associated with changes in circulating levels of various molecules, some of which remain undefined. We find that concentrations of circulating taurine decline with aging in mice, monkeys, and humans. A reversal of this decline through taurine supplementation increased the health span (the period of healthy living) and life span in mice and health span in monkeys. Mechanistically, taurine reduced cellular senescence, protected against telomerase deficiency, suppressed mitochondrial dysfunction, decreased DNA damage, and attenuated inflammaging. In humans, lower taurine concentrations correlated with several age-related diseases and taurine concentrations increased after acute endurance exercise. Thus, taurine deficiency may be a driver of aging because its reversal increases health span in worms, rodents, and primates and life span in worms and rodents. Clinical trials in humans seem warranted to test whether taurine deficiency might drive aging in humans.

studies.title: Taurine supplementation enhances endurance capacity by delaying blood glucose decline during prolonged exercise in rats.
studies.abstract: Taurine enhances physical performance; however, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. This study examined the effect of taurine on the overtime dynamics of blood glucose concentration (BGC) during endurance exercise in rats. Male F344 rats were subjected to transient treadmill exercise until exhaustion following 3 weeks of taurine supplementation or non-supplementation (TAU and CON groups). Every 10 min during exercise, BGC was measured in blood collected through cannulation of the jugular vein. Gluconeogenesis-, lipolysis-, and fatty acid oxidation-related factors in the plasma, liver, and skeletal muscles were also analyzed after 120-min run. Exercise time to exhaustion was significantly longer with taurine supplementation. BGC in the two groups significantly increased by 40 min and gradually and significantly decreased toward the respective exhaustion point. The decline in BGC from the peak at 40 min was significantly slower in the TAU group. The time when the once-increased BGC regressed to the 0-time level was significantly and positively correlated with exercise time until exhaustion. At the 120-min point, where the difference in BGC between the two groups was most significant, plasma free fatty acid concentration and acetyl-carnitine and N-acetyltaurine concentrations in skeletal muscle were significantly higher in the TAU group, whereas glycogen and glucogenic amino acid concentrations and G6Pase activity in the liver were not different between the two groups. Taurine supplementation enhances endurance capacity by delaying the decrease in BGC toward exhaustion through increases of lipolysis in adipose tissues and fatty acid oxidation in skeletal muscles during endurance exercise.

studies.title: Effects of Taurine-, Caffeine-, and Phosphatidylserine-Containing Supplementation Protocols on Physical and Cognitive Performance in Professional Male Football
studies.abstract: Background: Nutritional supplementation is widely used to support physical and cognitive performance in football. However, evidence on multi-ingredient protocols combining taurine, caffeine, and phosphatidylserine (PS) remains limited in professional athletes. Methods: Eighty-one professional male football players (19-32 years) were randomly assigned to three groups (n = 27): placebo (P), taurine + caffeine (TC; 1500 mg taurine + 200 mg caffeine), and taurine + caffeine + PS (TCP; 1500 mg taurine + 150 mg caffeine + 300 mg PS) in a randomized, placebo-controlled, single-blind trial. Supplementation lasted 10 days, with a final dose administered 60 min before a standardized 105 min training session. Reaction time, sprint performance, GPS-derived variables, and technical/tactical indicators were assessed. Data were analyzed using ANOVA with post hoc tests, and pairwise comparisons were additionally adjusted using the Holm-Bonferroni correction due to the exploratory nature of the analysis. Results: Compared with placebo, the TCP group was associated with more favorable physical, cognitive, and selected game-related outcomes (p < 0.05). TCP was associated with higher locomotor performance (η2 = 0.13-0.20) and smaller fatigue-related declines in sprint performance (-18% vs. -34%) and speed (-10% vs. -19%) (η2 = 0.18-0.22). Reaction time and technical indicators, including passing accuracy (84% vs. 75%) and dribbling success (73% vs. 62%), were also improved. Higher coach-rated tactical performance scores were observed in TCP (η2 = 0.19-0.25). Conclusions: A short-term multi-ingredient protocol including taurine, caffeine, and PS may be associated with improved physical, cognitive, and selected game-related outcomes in professional football players. However, due to differences in caffeine dosage between groups, the independent effect of PS cannot be determined. Further double-blind studies are warranted. Given the exploratory nature of the analysis, the multiple assessed outcomes, and the partly subjective coach-rated tactical evaluations, the cognitive and tactical findings should be interpreted cautiously and regarded as preliminary rather than confirmatory evidence.

studies.title: Effects of Taurine Supplementation on Vascular Endothelial Function at Rest and After Resistance Exercise.
studies.abstract: High-intensity resistance exercise has been shown to increase arterial stiffness and reduce vascular endothelial function. Taurine supplementation has a favorable effect on maintaining vascular function. We had previously reported that taurine supplementation attenuated increases in resistance exercise-induced arterial stiffness. In the present study, we further investigate the effects of taurine supplementation on vascular endothelial function at rest and after resistance exercise.Twenty-nine healthy men were recruited and randomly assigned to either the placebo supplement group (n = 14) or the taurine supplement group (n = 15) in a double-blinded manner. Subjects were required to ingest 6 g of either a placebo or the taurine supplement for 2 weeks prior to and 3 days following the exercise. Two weeks after the commencement of supplementation, the subjects were asked to perform 2 sets of 20 repetitive unilateral maximal-effort resistance exercise of the elbow flexors on a Biodex isokinetic dynamometer, with each contraction lasting 3 s, with 1 repetition performed every 9 s and 4 min rest in between sets. We evaluated the changes in brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD) in the non-exercised arm as an index of vascular endothelial function. Relative and absolute FMDs were measured prior to supplementation, before exercise, and 24, 48, and 96 h after exercise.Two weeks of taurine supplementation significantly increased both relative and absolute FMDs. Baseline diameter significantly increased at 96 h following the exercise in both groups. However, there was no change in the peak diameter. Consequently, both relative and absolute FMDs were significantly reduced at 96 h after the exercise in both groups. Taurine supplementation does not affect resistance exercise-induced reduction in FMD.Two weeks of taurine supplementation (6 g/day) significantly increased vascular endothelial function at rest; however, taurine supplementation did not improve resistance exercise-induced reduction in FMD.

B[La] was higher in taurine compared to placebo post-ramp (P = 0.004; d = 4.7). Taurine-lowered pre-exercise HR and improved incremental end-test power output, with subsequent detrimental effects on sprint performance, independent of cadence. Short endurance performance can be acutely enhanced after taurine ingestion but this effect might not be maintained across longer periods of exercise or induce the need for longer recovery periods.

studies.title: Effects of different doses of taurine supplementation on repeated-sprint performance after exhaustive exercise in a high temperature and humidity environment.
studies.abstract:
Objective

This study investigated the effects of acute pre-exercise taurine supplementation at different doses on exercise performance during exhaustive exercise and subsequent repeated sprint (RS; 6 sprints) activity in a high temperature and high humidity (HTHM) environment.

Methods

Sixteen college students (8 males and 8 females) participated in a single-blind, randomized, crossover-controlled trial. Participants completed four experimental conditions: high-dose taurine (HDG, 6g), medium-dose taurine (MDG, 4g), low-dose taurine (LDG, 1g), and placebo (PG). Sports performance, physiological responses, and subjective perceptions were assessed, including peak power (PP), mean power (MP), fatigue index (FI), reverse vertical jump (RVJ) height, time to exhaustion (ET), heart rate (HR), blood lactate (BLA), and rating of perceived exertion (RPE).

Results

During RS, PP and MP declined progressively across sprints (P < 0.05). Taurine supplementation attenuated the decline in power output compared with PG. In males, the HDG showed greater preservation of PP and MP, whereas in females, the LDG was more effective in maintaining MP, and the PG exhibited the greatest reduction in power output. Taurine supplementation increased exercise tolerance in a dose- and sex-dependent manner. ET was significantly longer in the HDG than in the PG in males, whereas in females, ET was significantly higher in the MDG compared with the PG (P < 0.05). RVJ performance decreased following exhaustive exercise in females (P < 0.05). Although no significant differences were observed in HR, BLA, or RPE among conditions, typical post-exercise response patterns were evident.

Conclusion

Acute taurine supplementation prolongs time to exhaustion and enhances repeated sprint performance in HTHM environment, with dose- and sex-specific effects.

Clinical trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06824571, January 22, 2025. Retrospectively registered.

studies.title: Effects of combined low-dose caffeine and taurine on anaerobic, neuromuscular, and cognitive performance: a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled crossover
studies.abstract: This study investigated the acute effects of low-dose caffeine (2 mg·kg⁻<sup>1</sup>) and taurine (10 mg·kg⁻<sup>1</sup>), administered alone and in combination, on anaerobic, neuromuscular, and cognitive performance in trained male athletes. Thirty-two participants, each with at least two years of consistent resistance training (≥ 3 sessions·week⁻<sup>1</sup>), completed experimental trials using a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover design following ingestion of caffeine, taurine, a caffeine-taurine combination, or placebo. Combined caffeine and taurine supplementation resulted in higher handgrip strength values compared to placebo [p = 0.044; d = 0.51, small effect] and greater average power than caffeine alone [p = 0.006; d = 0.64, moderate effect] and placebo [p = 0.001; d = 0.91, moderate effect]. Taurine supplementation alone did not significantly affect performance outcomes. No statistically significant differences were observed among conditions for peak power, cognitive performance, ratings of perceived exertion, or blood lactate concentrations (p > 0.05). Overall, these findings suggest that co-ingestion of low-dose caffeine and taurine may provide modest improvements in selected neuromuscular and anaerobic performance outcomes without affecting cognitive, perceptual, or metabolic responses. studies.title: Taurine supplementation enhances endurance capacity by delaying blood glucose decline during prolonged exercise in rats.
studies.abstract: Taurine enhances physical performance; however, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. This study examined the effect of taurine on the overtime dynamics of blood glucose concentration (BGC) during endurance exercise in rats. Male F344 rats were subjected to transient treadmill exercise until exhaustion following 3 weeks of taurine supplementation or non-supplementation (TAU and CON groups). Every 10 min during exercise, BGC was measured in blood collected through cannulation of the jugular vein. Gluconeogenesis-, lipolysis-, and fatty acid oxidation-related factors in the plasma, liver, and skeletal muscles were also analyzed after 120-min run. Exercise time to exhaustion was significantly longer with taurine supplementation. BGC in the two groups significantly increased by 40 min and gradually and significantly decreased toward the respective exhaustion point. The decline in BGC from the peak at 40 min was significantly slower in the TAU group. The time when the once-increased BGC regressed to the 0-time level was significantly and positively correlated with exercise time until exhaustion. At the 120-min point, where the difference in BGC between the two groups was most significant, plasma free fatty acid concentration and acetyl-carnitine and N-acetyltaurine concentrations in skeletal muscle were significantly higher in the TAU group, whereas glycogen and glucogenic amino acid concentrations and G6Pase activity in the liver were not different between the two groups. Taurine supplementation enhances endurance capacity by delaying the decrease in BGC toward exhaustion through increases of lipolysis in adipose tissues and fatty acid oxidation in skeletal muscles during endurance exercise.

explanation.what_it_is_line: A small amino acid found in meat and fish; made synthetically for supplements.
explanation.what_it_is: Taurine is a small organic compound (technically an amino acid, the building block of proteins) with the chemical formula C₂H₇NO₃S. Unlike most amino acids, your body can make its own taurine, but you also get it from eating meat, seafood, and eggs. It's naturally abundant in animal tissues, especially muscle and brain. People take it as an oral supplement, usually in powder or capsule form at doses ranging from a few hundred to several grams per day.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Supports cellular energy, reduces inflammation, and protects cells from oxidative damage.
explanation.how_it_works: Taurine works through several overlapping pathways. First, it helps regulate how cells produce and use energy, particularly in muscle and heart tissue — it can cross cell membranes and assist in the movement of minerals like calcium and potassium, which are critical for muscle contraction and nerve signaling. Second, it acts as an antioxidant, meaning it neutralizes harmful molecules called free radicals that damage cells; it also boosts your cells' own antioxidant defenses by supporting enzymes like taurine transporter proteins. Third, it reduces inflammation by modulating immune cell activity and lowering levels of inflammatory signaling molecules (cytokines). Because of these roles in energy, protection, and inflammation, taurine has been hypothesized to improve how muscles work during exercise, how the body handles blood sugar, and how cholesterol is managed — though the size of these effects in humans remains uncertain.
explanation.safety_line: Short-term use well-tolerated in trials; long-term safety and excluded populations not adequately tested.
explanation.safety_detail: The retrieved trials, most lasting weeks to a few months, reported few or no adverse events in adult participants taking taurine orally. However, nearly all studies excluded specific populations (pregnant women, children, people with kidney disease, those on blood-thinning medications), so safety in those groups remains untested. The evidence base is too narrow and short-term to claim overall safety.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety (years of daily use) has not been adequately tested in the retrieved records.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: excluded from nearly all trials — effects on mother or fetus unknown.
Kidney disease: taurine is metabolized by kidneys, so use in renal impairment is untested and potentially risky.
Children and adolescents: largely absent from retrieved studies; whether supplementation is safe or needed in young people is unknown.
explanation.chem_meaning: Taurine is extremely water-loving (XLogP –4.1, meaning it dissolves readily in water but poorly in fats), so it stays in the bloodstream and inside cells rather than accumulating in fatty tissues. This hydrophilic nature makes it easy to absorb orally and excrete via urine, which is why it has a low accumulation risk. Its small size (molecular weight 125) and charged sulfonic acid group allow it to cross cell membranes via specific transporters, enabling it to reach the inside of muscle, heart, and nerve cells where it does its work.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human studies (including two primary RCTs and four meta-analyses/systematic reviews) examined whether taurine supplementation improves blood sugar control and metabolic health. A 2022 meta-analysis of taurine's effects on diabetes mellitus, a 2026 meta-analysis on metabolic health in overweight/obese adults, and a 2026 clinical trial on metabolic health in healthcare workers (n=80) were among the human records retrieved. A 2026 meta-analysis of long-COVID patients (n=308) also examined glycemic markers. Most studies lasted weeks to months, and sample sizes ranged from 80 to over 300, though precise totals were not uniformly reported. Animal studies (18 records) consistently showed taurine reduced blood sugar levels and improved insulin signaling in rodent diabetes models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The human evidence base includes only two dedicated primary trials and four pooled analyses — below the threshold for a strong rating. Sample sizes and study durations are modest, and consistency across trials has not been independently verified, so confidence remains moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies (one primary observational trial and three meta-analyses) examined lipid profiles. A 1988 observational study in cystic fibrosis patients (n=10) found taurine supplementation affected fat absorption. Two 2026 meta-analyses examined cardiometabolic risk factors and long-COVID patients (n=308), and a 2018 meta-analysis on taurine's effects on growth and lipids in low-birthweight infants were retrieved. A small animal study (n=102) examined egg-laying hens' cholesterol and polyunsaturated fatty acids, and two other animal records assessed hepatic cholesterol metabolism. Human trial durations and sample sizes were generally modest, with verified totals around 420 participants across three studies reporting numbers explicitly.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one primary human trial and three pooled analyses exist in the retrieved records — below the strong evidence threshold. Precision is limited, consistency has not been independently replicated, and some studies were in narrow populations (infants, cystic fibrosis), limiting generalizability.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human studies (one meta-analysis and six RCTs) examined whether taurine improves aerobic endurance capacity. A 2018 meta-analysis synthesized the evidence, while individual trials tested endurance cycling performance in the heat (2019), maximal fat oxidation in recreational runners (2025), combined aerobic-resistance training effects (2026, n=11), and repeated-sprint performance (2018, 2026). A 2019 RCT measured vascular endothelial function at rest and after resistance exercise (n=15). Three animal studies examined endurance-related metabolism in rodents. Most human trials lasted 1–4 weeks and enrolled 11–15 participants per study, though the meta-analysis likely reviewed larger pooled cohorts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single meta-analysis exists but has not been independently verified or replicated by other systematic reviews in the retrieved records. Individual trial sample sizes are very small (~11–15 participants per arm), so effect estimates are imprecise. The consistency criterion is unmet, holding the grade at moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight human studies (one meta-analysis and seven RCTs) examined whether taurine enhances physical performance and training adaptations. A 2018 meta-analysis synthesized evidence; individual trials tested vascular function and resistance exercise (2019, n=15), irisin levels in obese women after high-intensity training (2019), repeat-sprint cycling in females (2018), and multi-ingredient supplementation protocols (2026). A 2026 clinical trial examined repeated-sprint performance after exhaustion at different doses. One animal study measured exercise-related physiology. Trial durations ranged from acute (single dose) to 4 weeks; most had 11–15 participants per group.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single meta-analysis provides the primary synthesis, but no independent replication of its findings appears in the retrieved records. Sample sizes are modest (~15 verified participants in the largest single trial), and most studies are acute or very short-term, limiting confidence in sustained effects. The grade remains moderate pending independent verification.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence is mixed human and animal, with moderate confidence. Human studies consist of two primary RCTs and four meta-analyses/systematic reviews (mostly 2022–2026, so recent), enrolling a cumulative ~700+ participants across all outcomes, though most individual trials are small (10–80 participants). Animal studies (18–24 per outcome) are consistent in direction but come from rodent models, which may not translate directly to humans. The human evidence base is too thin (few primary trials, below-threshold sample sizes) to reach strong confidence, placing all outcomes at moderate.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records do not include studies in children, pregnant women, or people with chronic kidney disease, so safety and efficacy in these groups are unknown. Most human trials lasted weeks to a few months — whether taurine's effects persist or accumulate over months to years of daily use has not been tested in the sample provided. Additionally, optimal dose and duration are not clearly established; trials used varying regimens (ranging from acute single doses to daily supplements over 4 weeks). The records show small, non-independent trial populations (often athletic or metabolically at-risk volunteers), so generalizability to the general adult population is unclear.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base relies heavily on animal studies (60–75% of retrieved trials per outcome) and very small human samples (median n=11–15 for exercise outcomes, only 1–2 primary human trials per lipid/glucose outcome), making it impossible to confidently predict clinical benefit in humans.

concerns.detail: For endurance and exercise performance, only 1 of 10 and 1 of 9 studies report sample sizes (n=11 and n=15 respectively). The engine notes these as 'modest verified sample' with 'unstable' effect estimates. A single outlier study or publication bias could easily reverse the apparent direction of effect, yet no pooled estimate is extractable to quantify uncertainty.

concerns.issue: Massive animal-to-human evidence ratio without validation
concerns.detail: Blood sugar (75% animal), cholesterol (75% animal), and endurance/exercise performance (30–90% animal depending on outcome) are dominated by animal models (C. elegans, canine hepatocytes, mice, broiler chickens, weanling pigs). Animal efficacy rarely translates directly to humans; the retrieved records show no evidence that the animal findings have been independently replicated in human trials or mechanistically validated in humans.

Blood sugar: 20 of 24 studies omit n; cholesterol: 13 of 16 studies omit n; endurance: 9 of 10 studies omit n. The engine estimates true total participants are 'substantially larger' than the 4 reported samples, but cannot verify this. This opacity prevents assessment of whether conclusions rest on large, well-powered trials or collections of tiny underpowered studies.

concerns.issue: Single meta-analysis per exercise outcome, unreplicated conclusion
concerns.detail: For endurance and exercise performance, the engine notes 'a single meta-analysis / systematic review exists, but its conclusion is not independently replicated or verified.' A meta-analysis can synthesize weak primary studies and amplify bias; without independent replication or a second systematic review with different inclusion criteria, there is no cross-check on whether the pooled finding is robust or an artifact of study selection.

concerns.issue: Recency clustering with no long-term safety data
concerns.detail: Most human trials are 2022–2026; lipids include only one 1988 observational study of 10 patients with cystic fibrosis. Recent clustering may reflect publication bias or growing interest without corresponding rigor. No long-term RCT safety data are evident (e.g., the 2025 animal study notes taurine 'induces hepatic steatosis and disrupts bile acid homeostasis'), and the absence of safety literature in these records is notable given the prevalence of supplementation.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Taurine is proposed to improve glucose metabolism via intracellular accumulation reduction (animal model), enhance endurance through delayed blood glucose decline, and modulate lipid metabolism and antioxidant capacity. These are plausible biochemical roles supported by cellular and animal data, but the inferential leap is substantial: glucose handling in C. elegans or broiler chickens does not directly predict glucose homeostasis in humans with diabetes, and animal antioxidant benefits do not necessarily translate to measurable clinical lipid or performance changes in free-living people. The mechanism is biologically coherent but the human dose, duration, and magnitude of effect remain unvalidated.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that (1) the human evidence base is almost entirely indirect: meta-analyses of small, heterogeneous trials (often combining taurine with other agents like caffeine or resistance training), and single-digit-sample RCTs unable to detect moderate effects; (2) the animal literature, while rich, shows mixed signals (e.g., one 2025 study reports taurine causes hepatic steatosis), suggesting non-monotonic or context-dependent effects; and (3) no independent replication of the single exercise meta-analysis exists, and the glucose/lipid meta-analyses are too recent to have spawned confirmatory meta-analyses. The 'Moderate' grade could reflect genuine modest benefit, or simply the absence of large, well-controlled human trials to definitively refute it.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A large (n≥200), adequately powered, multicenter RCT in a well-defined population (e.g., adults with prediabetes or sedentary individuals seeking endurance improvement) with pre-registered outcomes, standardized taurine dose, and 6–12 month follow-up would directly test whether any of these outcomes show clinically meaningful benefit in humans. Additionally, independent replication of the exercise meta-analysis using different databases or inclusion criteria would validate whether the apparent benefit is robust or an artifact of methodological choices.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un aminoácido pequeño que se encuentra en la carne y el pescado; se sintetiza para suplementos.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La taurina es un compuesto orgánico pequeño (técnicamente un aminoácido, el bloque de construcción de las proteínas) con la fórmula química C₂H₇NO₃S. A diferencia de la mayoría de los aminoácidos, tu cuerpo puede producir su propia taurina, pero también la obtienes al comer carne, mariscos y huevos. Se encuentra naturalmente en abundancia en los tejidos animales, especialmente en el músculo y el cerebro. Las personas la toman como suplemento oral, generalmente en forma de polvo o cápsula en dosis que van desde unos pocos cientos hasta varios gramos por día.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Apoya la energía celular, reduce la inflamación y protege las células del daño oxidativo.
explanation_es.how_it_works: La taurina actúa a través de varios caminos superpuestos. Primero, ayuda a regular cómo las células producen y utilizan energía, particularmente en el tejido muscular y cardíaco — puede cruzar las membranas celulares y ayudar en el movimiento de minerales como el calcio y el potasio, que son críticos para la contracción muscular y la señalización nerviosa. Segundo, actúa como un antioxidante, lo que significa que neutraliza moléculas dañinas llamadas radicales libres que dañan las células; también potencia las defensas antioxidantes propias de tus células apoyando enzimas como las proteínas transportadoras de taurina. Tercero, reduce la inflamación modulando la actividad de las células inmunitarias y reduciendo los niveles de moléculas de señalización inflamatoria (citocinas). Debido a estos roles en la energía, la protección y la inflamación, se ha propuesto que la taurina mejora cómo funcionan los músculos durante el ejercicio, cómo el cuerpo maneja el azúcar en la sangre y cómo se gestiona el colesterol — aunque el tamaño de estos efectos en humanos sigue siendo incierto.
explanation_es.safety_line: El uso a corto plazo se tolera bien en ensayos; la seguridad a largo plazo y en poblaciones excluidas no ha sido adecuadamente probada.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos recuperados, la mayoría durando semanas a unos pocos meses, reportaron pocos o ningún evento adverso en participantes adultos que tomaban taurina por vía oral. Sin embargo, casi todos los estudios excluyeron poblaciones específicas (mujeres embarazadas, niños, personas con enfermedad renal, aquellos en medicamentos anticoagulantes), por lo que la seguridad en esos grupos sigue siendo no probada. La base de evidencia es demasiado estrecha y a corto plazo para afirmar la seguridad general.
safety_bullets: La seguridad a largo plazo (años de uso diario) no ha sido adecuadamente probada en los registros recuperados.
Embarazo y lactancia: excluidos de casi todos los ensayos — los efectos en la madre o el feto son desconocidos.
Enfermedad renal: la taurina es metabolizada por los riñones, por lo que su uso en insuficiencia renal no ha sido probado y es potencialmente riesgoso.
Niños y adolescentes: en gran medida ausentes de los estudios recuperados; si la suplementación es segura o necesaria en personas jóvenes es desconocido.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La taurina es extremadamente amante del agua (XLogP –4.1, lo que significa que se disuelve fácilmente en agua pero mal en grasas), por lo que permanece en el torrente sanguíneo y dentro de las células en lugar de acumularse en los tejidos adiposos. Esta naturaleza hidrófila la hace fácil de absorber por vía oral y excretar mediante la orina, por lo que tiene bajo riesgo de acumulación. Su tamaño pequeño (peso molecular 125) y su grupo sulfónico cargado le permiten cruzar las membranas celulares a través de transportadores específicos, permitiéndole llegar al interior de las células musculares, cardíacas y nerviosas donde realiza su trabajo.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seis estudios humanos (incluyendo dos RCTs primarios y cuatro metanálisis/revisiones sistemáticas) examinaron si la suplementación con taurina mejora el control de la glucosa en sangre y la salud metabólica. Un metanálisis de 2022 sobre los efectos de la taurina en la diabetes mellitus, un metanálisis de 2026 sobre la salud metabólica en adultos con sobrepeso/obesidad, y un ensayo clínico de 2026 sobre la salud metabólica en trabajadores de la salud (n=80) fueron entre los registros humanos recuperados. Un metanálisis de 2026 de pacientes con COVID prolongado (n=308) también examinó marcadores glucémicos. La mayoría de los estudios duraron semanas a meses, y los tamaños de muestra oscilaron entre 80 y más de 300, aunque los totales precisos no fueron reportados uniformemente. Los estudios en animales (18 registros) mostraron consistentemente que la taurina redujo los niveles de azúcar en sangre y mejoró la señalización de insulina en modelos de diabetes en roedores.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La base de evidencia humana incluye solo dos ensayos primarios dedicados y cuatro análisis agrupados — por debajo del umbral para una calificación fuerte. Los tamaños de muestra y las duraciones de los estudios son modestos, y la consistencia entre ensayos no ha sido verificada de forma independiente, por lo que la confianza sigue siendo moderada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cuatro estudios humanos (un ensayo observacional primario y tres metanálisis) examinaron perfiles de lípidos. Un estudio observacional de 1988 en pacientes con fibrosis quística (n=10) encontró que la suplementación con taurina afectó la absorción de grasa. Dos metanálisis de 2026 examinaron factores de riesgo cardiometabólico y pacientes con COVID prolongado (n=308), y se recuperó un metanálisis de 2018 sobre los efectos de la taurina en el crecimiento y los lípidos en bebés de bajo peso al nacer. Un pequeño estudio en animales (n=102) examinó el colesterol y los ácidos grasos poliinsaturados en gallinas ponedoras, y otros dos registros en animales evaluaron el metabolismo del colesterol hepático. Las duraciones de los ensayos humanos y los tamaños de muestra fueron generalmente modestos, con totales verificados alrededor de 420 participantes en tres estudios que reportaron números explícitamente.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo existe un ensayo humano primario y tres análisis agrupados en los registros recuperados — por debajo del umbral de evidencia fuerte. La precisión es limitada, la consistencia no ha sido replicada de forma independiente, y algunos estudios fueron en poblaciones estrechas (bebés, fibrosis quística), limitando la generalizabilidad.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Siete estudios humanos (un metanálisis y seis RCTs) examinaron si la taurina mejora la capacidad de resistencia aeróbica. Un metanálisis de 2018 sintetizó la evidencia, mientras que ensayos individuales probaron el rendimiento en ciclismo de resistencia en el calor (2019), la oxidación máxima de grasas en corredores recreativos (2025), los efectos del entrenamiento aeróbico-resistencia combinado (2026, n=11), y el rendimiento en esfuerzos repetidos (2018, 2026). Un RCT de 2019 midió la función del endotelio vascular en reposo y después del ejercicio de resistencia (n=15). Tres estudios en animales examinaron el metabolismo relacionado con la resistencia en roedores. La mayoría de los ensayos humanos duraron 1–4 semanas e inscribieron 11–15 participantes por estudio, aunque el metanálisis probablemente revisó cohortes agrupadas más grandes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existe un único metanálisis pero no ha sido verificado o replicado de forma independiente por otras revisiones sistemáticas en los registros recuperados. Los tamaños de muestra de los ensayos individuales son muy pequeños (~11–15 participantes por brazo), por lo que las estimaciones de efecto son imprecisas. El criterio de consistencia no se cumple, manteniendo la calificación en moderada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ocho estudios humanos (un metanálisis y siete RCTs) examinaron si la taurina mejora el rendimiento físico y las adaptaciones al entrenamiento. Un metanálisis de 2018 sintetizó la evidencia; ensayos individuales probaron la función vascular y el ejercicio de resistencia (2019, n=15), niveles de irisina en mujeres obesas después de entrenamiento de alta intensidad (2019), ciclismo de esfuerzos repetidos en mujeres (2018), y protocolos de suplementación multiingrediente (2026). Un ensayo clínico de 2026 examinó el rendimiento en esfuerzos repetidos después del agotamiento a diferentes dosis. Un estudio en animales midió la fisiología relacionada con el ejercicio. Las duraciones de los ensayos oscilaron entre agudas (dosis única) a 4 semanas; la mayoría tuvo 11–15 participantes por grupo.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Un único metanálisis proporciona la síntesis primaria, pero no aparece replicación independiente de sus hallazgos en los registros recuperados. Los tamaños de muestra son modestos (~15 participantes verificados en el ensayo más grande individual), y la mayoría de los estudios son agudos o muy a corto plazo, limitando la confianza en efectos sostenidos. La calificación se mantiene en moderada en espera de verificación independiente.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La evidencia es mixta en humanos y animales, con confianza moderada. Los estudios humanos consisten en dos RCTs primarios y cuatro metanálisis/revisiones sistemáticas (principalmente 2022–2026, por lo que recientes), inscribiendo un total acumulado de ~700+ participantes en todos los resultados, aunque la mayoría de los ensayos individuales son pequeños (10–80 participantes). Los estudios en animales (18–24 por resultado) son consistentes en dirección pero provienen de modelos en roedores, que podrían no traducirse directamente a humanos. La base de evidencia humana es demasiado delgada (pocos ensayos primarios, tamaños de muestra por debajo del umbral) para alcanzar confianza fuerte, colocando todos los resultados en moderada.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados no incluyen estudios en niños, mujeres embarazadas o personas con enfermedad renal crónica, por lo que la seguridad y la eficacia en estos grupos son desconocidas. La mayoría de los ensayos humanos duraron semanas a unos pocos meses — si los efectos de la taurina persisten o se acumulan durante meses a años de uso diario no ha sido probado en la muestra proporcionada. Además, la dosis y duración óptimas no están claramente establecidas; los ensayos utilizaron regímenes variados (que van desde dosis únicas agudas a suplementos diarios durante 4 semanas). Los registros muestran poblaciones pequeñas y no independientes en los ensayos (frecuentemente voluntarios atletas o con riesgo metabólico), por lo que la generalizabilidad a la población adulta general es poco clara.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia se basa en gran medida en estudios animales (60–75% de los ensayos recuperados por resultado) y muestras humanas muy pequeñas (mediana n=11–15 para resultados de ejercicio, solo 1–2 ensayos primarios humanos por resultado de lípidos/glucosa), lo que hace imposible predecir con confianza el beneficio clínico en humanos.

concerns.issue: Imprecisión severa en resultados de ejercicio
concerns.detail: Para resistencia y desempeño del ejercicio, solo 1 de 10 y 1 de 9 estudios reportan tamaños de muestra (n=11 y n=15 respectivamente). El motor los señala como 'muestra modesta verificada' con estimaciones de efecto 'inestables'. Un único estudio atípico o sesgo de publicación podría fácilmente revertir la dirección aparente del efecto, sin embargo, no hay estimado combinado extractable para cuantificar la incertidumbre.

concerns.issue: Proporción masiva de evidencia animal-a-humana sin validación
concerns.detail: Azúcar en sangre (75% animal), colesterol (75% animal) y resistencia/desempeño del ejercicio (30–90% animal dependiendo del resultado) están dominados por modelos animales (C. elegans, hepatocitos caninos, ratones, pollos de engorde, lechones destetados). La eficacia animal rara vez se traduce directamente en humanos; los registros recuperados no muestran evidencia de que los hallazgos animales hayan sido replicados independientemente en ensayos humanos o validados mecánicamente en humanos.

concerns.issue: Subnotificación extrema de tamaños de muestra
concerns.detail: Azúcar en sangre: 20 de 24 estudios omiten n; colesterol: 13 de 16 estudios omiten n; resistencia: 9 de 10 estudios omiten n. El motor estima que los verdaderos participantes totales son 'sustancialmente mayores' que las 4 muestras reportadas, pero no puede verificarlo. Esta falta de transparencia impide evaluar si las conclusiones se basan en ensayos grandes y bien potenciados o en colecciones de estudios diminutos sin poder estadístico.

concerns.issue: Único metanálisis por resultado de ejercicio, conclusión no replicada
concerns.detail: Para resistencia y desempeño del ejercicio, el motor señala que 'existe un único metanálisis / revisión sistemática, pero su conclusión no está replicada o verificada independientemente'. Un metanálisis puede sintetizar estudios primarios débiles y amplificar sesgos; sin replicación independiente o una segunda revisión sistemática con criterios de inclusión diferentes, no hay verificación cruzada sobre si el hallazgo combinado es robusto o un artefacto de la selección de estudios.

concerns.issue: Agrupamiento por recencia sin datos de seguridad a largo plazo
concerns.detail: La mayoría de los ensayos humanos son 2022–2026; lípidos incluyen solo un estudio observacional de 1988 de 10 pacientes con fibrosis quística. El agrupamiento reciente puede reflejar sesgo de publicación o interés creciente sin rigor correspondiente. No hay evidencia clara de datos de seguridad en ensayos clínicos aleatorizados a largo plazo (p. ej., el estudio animal de 2025 señala que la taurina 'induce esteatosis hepática y disrupta la homeostasis del ácido biliar'), y la ausencia de literatura de seguridad en estos registros es notable dada la prevalencia de suplementación.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: Se propone que la taurina mejore el metabolismo de la glucosa mediante la reducción de la acumulación intracelular (modelo animal), mejore la resistencia mediante la reducción retrasada de glucosa en sangre, y module el metabolismo de lípidos y la capacidad antioxidante. Estos son roles bioquímicos plausibles apoyados por datos celulares y animales, pero el salto inferencial es sustancial: el manejo de glucosa en C. elegans o pollos de engorde no predice directamente la homeostasis de glucosa en humanos con diabetes, y los beneficios antioxidantes animales no necesariamente se traducen en cambios clínicos medibles de lípidos o desempeño en personas en vida libre. El mecanismo es biológicamente coherente pero la dosis humana, duración y magnitud del efecto permanecen sin validar.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que (1) la base de evidencia humana es casi enteramente indirecta: metanálisis de ensayos pequeños y heterogéneos (frecuentemente combinando taurina con otros agentes como cafeína o entrenamiento de resistencia), y ensayos clínicos aleatorizados con muestras de un dígito incapaces de detectar efectos moderados; (2) la literatura animal, aunque extensa, muestra señales mixtas (p. ej., un estudio de 2025 reporta que la taurina causa esteatosis hepática), sugiriendo efectos no monotónicos o dependientes del contexto; y (3) no existe replicación independiente del único metanálisis de ejercicio, y los metanálisis de glucosa/lípidos son demasiado recientes para haber generado metanálisis confirmatorios. La calificación 'Moderada' podría reflejar un beneficio genuino modesto, o simplemente la ausencia de ensayos humanos grandes y bien controlados para refutarlo definitivamente.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ensayo clínico aleatorizado grande (n≥200), adecuadamente potenciado, multicéntrico en una población bien definida (p. ej., adultos con prediabetes o individuos sedentarios que buscan mejora de resistencia) con resultados pre-registrados, dosis estandarizada de taurina y seguimiento de 6–12 meses probaría directamente si alguno de estos resultados muestra beneficio clínicamente significativo en humanos. Además, la replicación independiente del metanálisis de ejercicio utilizando bases de datos diferentes o criterios de inclusión diferentes validaría si el beneficio aparente es robusto o un artefacto de las decisiones metodológicas.
